name: Gum grafting

lead: Gum grafting is a periodontal surgery that places tissue, most often from the roof of the mouth, over exposed roots or at sites with thin gum. It is used to cover recession and to build a thicker gum band.
The sources reviewed describe the techniques and ongoing trials but give few published outcome figures.

paras: Tissue from the palate, neighbouring gum or a donor matrix is positioned and sutured at the recession site, and heals in place over roughly two to four weeks.
Palatal donor-site healing and discomfort are the subject of several trials. Detailed complication rates were not available in the sources reviewed.

lead: Gum grafting is a periodontal plastic surgery in which gum tissue, usually taken from the palate or from a donor source, is placed at a site with gum recession or too little keratinised tissue. It is used to cover exposed roots and to thicken or widen the gum band, including cosmetically.[1][2]

Common types include pedicle grafts that move nearby tissue, free gingival grafts, subepithelial connective tissue grafts and acellular dermal matrix as an alternative to palate tissue.[3] Healing is reported to take about 2 to 4 weeks.[3] Much of the current research concerns palatal donor-site healing and keratinised tissue around implants.[4][5]

paras: A pedicle graft moves tissue next to the recession over the exposed root. A free gingival graft or subepithelial connective tissue graft uses tissue from the palate, and an acellular dermal matrix is a processed donated skin product used instead of the patient's own tissue.[3] A 1997 article described cosmetic gum grafting.[2]

Besides covering recessions, grafts are used where keratinised tissue is limited. A 2026 case study described placing a free gingival graft before a regenerative procedure at a site with limited keratinised tissue.[1]

Registered trials compare a gingival unit graft with a free gingival graft over 18 months,[6] test wound-healing products and techniques at the palatal donor site,[7][8][9] examine keratinised mucosa and soft-tissue health around implants,[10][11] and compare graft harvesting techniques in recession sites.[12] Published results are not summarised here. Clinical evidence in the sources reviewed is otherwise limited to a case study.[1]

Palatal donor-site wound healing, pain and comfort are themselves the subject of trials, indicating the donor site is a recognised source of morbidity.[7][8] Encyclopedic sources do not detail risks of grafting.[3]
